claim_summary: A federal appeals court allowed USCIS to resume re-reviewing previously approved immigration benefits for certain nationals from travel-ban countries who entered the United States on or after 20 January 2021, while litigation continues.
instrument: First Circuit Order of Court, No. 26-1703, entered 14 August 2026, granting a partial stay pending appeal of the Rule 54(b) judgment in Dorcas International Institute of Rhode Island v. USCIS, No. 1:26-cv-00132-JJM-PAS (D.R.I., 11 June 2026). The underlying agency instruments are USCIS policy memoranda PM-602-0192 (2 December 2025) and PM-602-0194 (1 January 2026) and Policy Alert PA-2025-26, none of which USCIS has published; they exist only in the certified administrative record.
quote_original: we grant defendants-appellants' request for stay, in part, limited to the Comprehensive Re-Review Policy. The request for stay is otherwise denied.
notes: True, with the date corrected: the stay was entered 14 August 2026, not 17 August (17 August is when the law firm reported it). Discovery source was a Fragomen bulletin, not authority; the instrument cited here is the court's own order. Three cautions. (1) The order is a partial stay of a stay, not a rule: only the Comprehensive Re-Review Policy is revived; the Benefits Hold Policy and Country-Specific Factors Policy remain vacated. (2) The lead's phrase 'travel ban countries' is imprecise — the D.R.I. memorandum says 'countries listed in Proclamation No. 10949' (verified quote at https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.rid.61671/gov.uscourts.rid.61671.28.0_1.pdf: 'conduct a comprehensive re-review of already approved benefit requests for individuals from countries listed in Proclamation No. 10949 who entered the United States on or after January 20, 2021.'), and the CA1 order itself brackets them as '[certain countries]'. (3) Provenance caveat: storage.courtlistener.com is a RECAP mirror of the court's filed PDF, not a .gov host. That is acceptable here only because nothing is being authored from it; if this ever becomes a recorded source it must be re-anchored to the court or to a USCIS publication. USCIS's own alert (https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/alerts/court-order-on-hold-policies) still says the three policies 'should be treated as if they are not in effect' and has not been updated for the 14 August partial stay. This touches no atlas route: it concerns re-opening already-granted benefits, not the terms of any citizenship or residence route. Interlocutory posture — the government's opening brief is due 10 September 2026.

claim_summary: Nicaragua amended its constitution to strip Nicaraguan nationality from citizens who acquire another nationality, while requiring naturalising foreigners to renounce their origin nationality, except Central Americans by origin.
instrument: Ley N°. 1268, Ley de Reforma Parcial a los Artículos 23 y 25 de la Constitución Política de la República de Nicaragua. Approved 14 January 2026, sanctioned 15 January 2026, published in La Gaceta, Diario Oficial N°. 09 of 16 January 2026, in force on publication.
quote_original: Artículo 25 La nacionalidad nicaragüense se perderá
quote_translation: Article 25. Nicaraguan nationality shall be lost [at the moment another nationality is acquired].
data_change_needed: Author the jurisdiction-level dual_nationality block for Nicaragua, which is currently null. provenance: instrument. retention.by_birth.effect and retention.by_naturalisation.effect: automatic_loss (art. 25 draws no distinction between nationals and nacionalizados). acquisition.effect: renunciation_with_exceptions (art. 23 para 1 requires prior renunciation of the origin nationality; para 2 exempts Central Americans by origin resident in Nicaragua). asymmetry: inbound carries a Central American exception, outbound carries none. source_refs: the La Gaceta N°. 09 PDF above. Separately, three corrections to existing rows: (a) nicaragua-naturalization cites 'Article 19' and nicaragua-central-american-option cites 'Article 17', both pre-2025 numbering — they are now art. 23 para 1 and art. 23 para 2; (b) all five Nicaragua routes are sourced to a constituteproject URL the records themselves label STALE, and constituteproject is a banned host in the quote gate — replace with the two Gaceta PDFs; (c) note that Ley 1268 deleted the former art. 23 third paragraph, so the treaty-and-reciprocity carve-out for dual nationality no longer exists.
notes: Confirmed on the primary instrument, and the change is a complete reversal that is provable in both directions. Pre-reform text, from the Texto Íntegro published as Ley N°. 1234 in La Gaceta, Diario Oficial N°. 32 of 18 February 2025 (http://digesto.asamblea.gob.ni/consultas/util/pdf.php?type=rdd&rdd=KSLWCOPwMeA%3D, quote verified character-for-character): 'Artículo 25   La calidad de nacional no se pierde por el hecho de adquirir otra nacionalidad.' — 'Article 25. The status of national is not lost by reason of acquiring another nationality.' Post-reform art. 25 reads in full: 'La nacionalidad nicaragüense se perderá al momento de adquirir otra nacionalidad.' Ley 1268 does three things: it changes art. 23 para 1 from 'previa renuncia a su nacionalidad' to 'previa renuncia a su nacionalidad originaria'; it deletes the former art. 23 para 3, 'En los casos de doble nacionalidad se procede conforme los tratados y el principio de reciprocidad'; and it reverses art. 25. The Central American exception in art. 23 para 2 survives unchanged, so nicaragua-central-american-option remains correct in substance. QUOTE-GATE MECHANICS, important: La Gaceta is printed in two columns and pdftotext -layout interleaves them, so the full art. 25 sentence does NOT match as one string. The recorded quote is the first physical line and matches. The continuation 'al momento de adquirir otra nacionalidad."' also matches independently if a second quote is wanted. The pre-reform quote from Gaceta N°. 32 matches whole. PUBLISHER MECHANICS: digesto.asamblea.gob.ni serves search and document lookup only by AJAX POST to /consultas/util/ws/proxy.php (hddQueryType=getJuridicNorms to find a norm, hddQueryType=getRddsByIunp to get its publication id), and shownorms.php returns a JS shell on a plain GET — this is what defeated earlier passes. The pdf.php?type=rdd&rdd=... URL recorded above IS a plain GET and is stable, so the gate can fetch it. The host is HTTP-only: HTTPS times out, so the http:// scheme is deliberate and must not be 'corrected'. The type=pdfIunp variant returns a 200 with zero bytes and must not be used. Discovery source was divergentes.com, a news outlet and not authority; it was used only to learn the law number, and its framing ('nicaragüenses que renuncien a su nacionalidad para adquirir otra') is looser than the enacted text, which makes loss automatic on acquisition rather than conditional on renunciation. The lead's own summary is the accurate one. This is the A4 rights-index fact the atlas most needs and the highest-value row in this batch.

claim_summary: An upcoming DHS webinar discusses new regulations introducing fixed periods of stay for F and J international students and exchange visitors.
instrument: None. A webinar announcement is not an instrument. The rule it discusses is the same final rule as issue 215: 'Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media', 91 FR 44976, RIN 1653-AA95.
quote_original: SEVP will host a live stakeholder webinar on Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, from 2 to 3 p.m. EDT to review major regulatory changes resulting from the final rule and answer frequently asked questions.
notes: Duplicate of issue 215 and should be closed as such — this is the answer to the question of whether the five US leads are one change or several. Discovery source was a Fragomen webcast invitation. The lead's date is also wrong: DHS/SEVP's own webinar is Monday 31 August 2026, per the verified quote; 2 September 2026 is the law firm's own webcast, not a DHS event. Nothing recordable: a webinar is not law, and the rule behind it is captured under issue 215.

claim_summary: A federal lawsuit was filed seeking to block a new final rule that eliminates admission for duration of status and replaces it with fixed periods of admission for F, J and I nonimmigrants.
instrument: Final rule, 'Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media', 91 FR 44976 (pp. 44976–45131), RIN 1653-AA95, DHS Docket No. ICEB-2025-0001, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Published 17 July 2026, effective 15 September 2026, amending 8 CFR Parts 214, 248 and 274a. The challenge is Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. DHS, No. 1:26-cv-13799 (D. Mass.), filed 18 August 2026 under the APA.
quote_original: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is amending its regulations to change the admission period in the F, J, and I classifications from duration of status to an admission for a fixed time period, and additional changes to admission and extension requirements.
notes: Both limbs verify: the rule and the lawsuit are real. This is the instrument behind issue 214, so 214 and 215 are ONE regulatory change, not two. No data change, because the atlas holds no F, J or I rows at all — every US row is E-2, EB-1A, EB-5, Gold Card, O-1 or one of the four citizenship routes. Whether to begin covering US nonimmigrant study and exchange statuses is a scope decision, not a lead fix, and should not be smuggled in through a monitor triage. Two things make the effective date soft, and either would invalidate a recorded figure: the rule is a CRA major rule, and its DATES section reserves the right to republish the effective date or terminate the rule after congressional review; and the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction or APA s.705 relief was filed on 18 August 2026 and is pending. The operative regulatory text, new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), also verifies at the same URL: 'An F-1 student is admitted for a fixed period of time, which is the period necessary to complete the course of study indicated on the Form I-20, or successor form, not to exceed a period of 4 years'. Transition is new 8 CFR 214.1(m): F and J holders properly maintaining duration-of-status admission on 15 September 2026 may remain to the later of their EAD expiry or program end date, capped at four years from 15 September 2026 plus a 60-day (F) or 30-day (J) departure period. Discovery source was a Fragomen bulletin; the lawsuit was not named in the lead and was located by full-text docket search. Fetch trap worth recording: the Federal Register raw-text file contains NUL bytes, which make grep treat it as binary and return nothing silently — a false negative that looks like an absent quote. The quote gate is unaffected because it decodes rather than greps.

claim_summary: From 18 August 2026, additional U.S. consular posts including Canada and Guatemala City joined a pilot offering B-1/B-2 visa appointments within 10 business days for an additional fee of USD 750.
instrument: Temporary final rule, 'Schedule of Fees for Consular Services, Department of State and Overseas Embassies and Consulates—Visa and Citizenship Services Fee Changes', 91 FR 34768, RIN 1400-AG13, docket DOS-2026-0727. Published 9 June 2026, effective 1 July 2026 through 31 December 2026, amending 22 CFR 22.1 to add Item 26, 'Nonimmigrant Visa Appointment Expedite Fee (per person) $750'. No Federal Register document announces the post expansion.
quote_original: This temporary final rule (TFR) temporarily amends the Schedule of Fees for Consular Services (Schedule) to create a $750 fee for an expedited B1/B2, business and tourism, nonimmigrant visa (NIV) interview appointment.
notes: Reported apart, because these are two different answers and must not be folded into one. VERIFIED on the instrument: the USD 750 fee, the ten-business-day window, the B-1/B-2 limitation, and the pilot structure. Also verified at the same URL: 'This temporary final rule is effective July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2026.' — it self-expires. CANNOT DETERMINE: the specific claim of this lead, namely that Canada, Bogota, Guatemala City, San Jose and Tegucigalpa joined on 18 August 2026. The TFR names no post at all; it delegates the list entirely to travel.state.gov, saying only 'The Bureau of Consular Affairs will control which embassies and consulates can offer this service.' That page could not be read. What was tried and how it failed, because this is a textbook 'a 200 proves nothing' case: travel.state.gov returns a Cloudflare 403 interstitial to both curl and WebFetch; www.state.gov and five usembassy.gov hosts (Canada, Colombia, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Honduras) each returned HTTP 200 with a byte-identical 659,508-byte 'Technical Difficulties' page, identical md5 across all six, so a status-code check alone would have reported a successful fetch of nothing; and the Wayback capture of the relevant travel.state.gov page archived the 403 rather than the content. Discovery source was a Fragomen bulletin. Even if the post list were readable this touches no atlas route — the atlas holds no B-1/B-2 rows, and a visitor-visa appointment-scheduling surcharge on a rule that expires on 31 December 2026 is operational, not a route term. Recommend closing unless the post list is wanted for its own sake, in which case it needs a rendered browser fetch of travel.state.gov.

claim_summary: Ghana enacted the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173), replacing the GIPC Act, revising capital investment thresholds and work-permit routing, and introducing a citizenship-by-investment category.
instrument: Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173). Date of assent and date of Gazette notification both 15 July 2026. Repeals and saves the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre Act, 2013 (Act 865) at s.60. Relevant provisions: s.31 minimum foreign capital, s.39 under the heading 'Citizenship by Investment', s.49 expatriate quotas, s.50 work permits.
quote_original: There is also the expansion of expatriate quota thresholds, a statutory mandate for outward investment promotion, the establishment of a One-Stop-Shop, citizenship–by–investment, and alignment with the AfCFTA Protocol on Investment and international best practices.
notes: The Act is real; the headline claim is false as stated. Act 1173 does NOT create a citizenship-by-investment programme. Section 39, read off the official Act PDF at https://gipc.gov.gh/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GIPA-ACT-2026.pdf, is a mandate to legislate later and confers nothing: 'The Ministry of the Interior shall, in consultation with the Authority and in accordance with the Constitution and any other applicable legislation, enact legislation relating to citizenship by investment.' No thresholds, no eligibility, no procedure, and no such legislation has been traced. Nor is this a confusion with the right of abode for investors under the Immigration Act, 2000 (Act 573) s.17 — Act 1173 contains no residence provision at all; its sections 48 to 51 are labour, expatriate quotas, work permit and assistance. Under the no-negatives rule there is nothing to record: authoring a Ghana investor-citizenship route would put a programme in the atlas that does not exist, and the absence belongs in this note. QUOTE PROVENANCE, and this is the load-bearing caveat: the Act PDF is a 44-page scan with NO text layer — pdftotext returns 44 bytes — so the s.39, assent, s.31, s.49 and s.50 texts were transcribed from page renders and CANNOT be matched character-for-character by the quote gate. Do not record any of them as a gated quote without OCR and a re-read. The quote recorded above is from the GIPA press release, which has a real text layer and does verify; note that it is the agency's own feature list, and its bare mention of 'citizenship–by–investment' is almost certainly what the EY bulletin was written from. Discovery source was EY, secondary; the agency's own site carries both the Act and the release, so EY is not needed as authority. parliament.gh returns a healthy 200 for its Acts listing but the dataset is stale legacy data ending around 2021 and contains no 2026 Act — another 200-proves-nothing surface. What IS recordable here is the expatriate-quota and work-permit change, which is neither a citizenship nor a residence route and so has no home in the current schema.

claim_summary: USCIS issued new public charge policy guidance taking effect 18 September 2026, changing the standard for adjustment of status applications to whether the applicant is likely to become dependent on means-tested public benefits for basic needs at any time.
instrument: Two linked instruments. Final rule 'Public Charge Ground of Inadmissibility', 91 FR 45324, RIN 1615-AD06, CIS No. 2857-26, DHS Docket No. USCIS-2025-0304, published 20 July 2026, effective 18 September 2026, amending 8 CFR Parts 103 and 212 and removing 8 CFR 212.20 to 212.23 — it rescinds the 2022 rule at 87 FR 55472 and codifies no replacement standard. USCIS Policy Alert PA-2026-09, 'Public Charge Ground of Inadmissibility', issued 18 August 2026, USCIS Policy Manual Volume 8 Part G, carries the operative test.
quote_original: officers must determine whether an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge, that is, likely at any time to depend on means-tested public benefits.
notes: Confirmed: the 18 September 2026 date and the substance of the new standard both check out on the primary sources, and the guidance's effective-date sentence verifies at the same URL — 'is effective on September 18, 2026, and applies to all applications for adjustment of status (unless exempt) postmarked or electronically submitted on or after that date.' The lead's own wording, 'dependent on means-tested public benefits for their basic needs', appears nowhere verbatim and must not be quoted as the standard; the guidance says the applicant is 'likely to become dependent on the government to meet his or her basic needs, for example shelter, food, or healthcare,' typically demonstrated through dependence on means-tested benefits. QUOTE-GATE MECHANICS: that longer sentence carries inline footnote markers 55 and 56 and a hyphenated line break at 'means-tested', so it does not match as a single string. The shorter sentence recorded above is footnote-free and matches. Discovery source was a Fragomen bulletin, not authority. No data change: the atlas has no public-charge or adjustment-of-status field, and this is an eligibility screen rather than a route term. It is the only one of the five US leads with any adjacency, since it applies to adjustment applicants including investors and priority workers — the population behind us-eb5-direct-investor, us-eb5-regional-center and us-eb1a-extraordinary-ability — but it changes none of those routes' recorded terms. Structural caution if this is ever recorded: DHS deliberately declined to codify the new test, so the standard lives in expressly non-binding subregulatory guidance, which commenters challenged under Perez v. Mortgage Bankers; it is the most litigation-exposed of the five. Transition is a benefit-vintage split — benefits received before 18 September 2026 are weighed under the 2022 rule, benefits received on or after count in full. Trap worth recording: https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-8-part-g/updates returns a 404 page under HTTP 200; the working index is /policy-manual/updates.

claim_summary: Jordan's Cabinet approved a revised investor citizenship and residency framework raising the minimum stock market investment threshold to JOD 1.5 million.
instrument: Cabinet decision of 15 July 2026 amending the criteria for granting Jordanian residency and citizenship to investors, announced by the Ministry of Investment. No gazette citation or numbered by-law reference is published on either official page.
quote_original: Jordanian citizenship may be granted to an investor who makes a new investment of no less than JOD 1.5 million in shares of Jordanian companies.
data_change_needed: Record the listed-shares threshold of JOD 1,500,000 on jordan-investor-citizenship, which currently has min_investment null and a pathway note that captures the four-month broker window, the five-year hold and the no-leverage terms but no securities figure. Do NOT record a 50 percent increase or a JOD 1,000,000 predecessor. Optionally also newly available from the same decision and not held: the Amrah City Project track at JOD 1.5 million; new-project paid-up capital of JOD 700,000 in the Capital Governorate against JOD 500,000 outside; existing-investment asset averages of JOD 700,000 in Amman against JOD 350,000 outside; employment tracks of 150 Jordanians in Amman and 100 in the governorates; and the family extension to spouse, dependent daughters, unmarried sons under 24 and dependent parents, extending to sons up to 30 with their own families above JOD 2 million.
notes: Split verdict, reported apart. The JOD 1.5 million securities threshold is real, confirmable at two official sources, and genuinely new to the atlas — this is the recordable part. Corroborated at the state news agency (https://petra.gov.jo/en/news/government-revamps-investor-citizenship-rules-to-funnel-capital-into-provinces, verified quote: 'To secure citizenship through the Amman Stock Exchange, foreign investors must now make a new purchase of shares in Jordanian companies valued at no less than 1.5 million dinars.'). The '50 percent increase from JOD 1 million' framing does NOT verify: neither official page states any prior figure, and both say only that the decision raises the threshold. The likely origin of the 1m-to-1.5m story is a different track in the same decision, where citizenship for acquiring equity in existing productive projects carries a JOD 1 million threshold — so the two figures are two tracks, not a before and after. The atlas already reflects this Cabinet decision: the jordan-investor-citizenship note records the 15 July 2026 property cut to JOD 150,000 outside Amman and the listed-shares broker and hold conditions, and both cited URLs resolve to real on-point content, so neither is fabricated. Only the securities figure is missing. Both quotes are from the official English editions. One integrity flag on the source: the invest.jo HTML carries data-start and data-end attributes throughout, a signature of machine-generated markup pasted into the CMS. The page is genuinely on the Ministry's domain, but if the figure is to be load-bearing, prefer the Arabic original.

claim_summary: Bahrain reduced the minimum real estate investment threshold for the Golden Residency visa from BHD 200,000 to BHD 130,000.
instrument: None obtained. No decree, resolution or gazette reference was located; the atlas's existing authority is the NPRA service page.
notes: The atlas already holds exactly this claim and the lead adds nothing. Residence route bahrain-golden-residency-property carries min_investment BHD 130,000, its title states '(BHD 130,000+, lowered from BHD 200,000)', it is sourced to the NPRA page above, last_checked 2026-07-30, confidence medium. Close as covered. EXPECT THIS ROW TO FAIL research:verify:quotes, and that failure is correct rather than a defect: quote_original is null because the source could not be re-read on this pass, so nothing is being asserted as verified today. The already-held evidence is the 2026-07-30 authoring pass, not this one. What was tried: npra.gov.bh timed out at TCP level over HTTPS and over plain HTTP, from every egress available, while DNS resolved normally to 85.158.131.217 — this is a network or geo block on the host, so the atlas source URL should NOT be presumed rotten; goldenresidency.gov.bh, a previously unrecorded official host dedicated to the programme, returns HTTP 405 behind an AWS WAF human-verification challenge and is the best candidate for a re-read from a real browser; www.bna.bh returned 405 behind the same WAF. Separately, the DISCOVERY URL IS EFFECTIVELY FABRICATED and must not be added as a source: https://www.bahrain.bh/wps/portal/en/meta/news/newsdetails/NPRA_GoldenResidency_InvestmentUpdate returns HTTP 200 with 144,908 bytes but silently serves the National Portal homepage, title 'Home', and the body contains no occurrence of 'Golden' or '130'. The portal serves its homepage for any unmatched /meta/news/newsdetails/ path — worth adding to the institutional list of 200-proves-nothing surfaces.

claim_summary: El Salvador reduced the mandatory physical presence requirement for temporary residents from nine months to 90 calendar days per year.
instrument: Decreto Legislativo N.º 531, Reformas a la Ley Especial de Migración y de Extranjería, issued 17 March 2026, published in Diario Oficial N.º 57, Tomo N.º 450, of 23 March 2026, in force eight days after publication (31 March 2026). Amends articles 49, 119, 164 and 279 of the Ley Especial de Migración y de Extranjería (Decreto Legislativo N.º 286 of 2 April 2019).
quote_original: Art.119.- Toda persona con residencia temporal deberá permanecer en el territorio salvadoreño un mínimo de noventa días calendario dentro de cada año, ya sean estos consecutivos o acumulados, salvo que exista caso fortuito o fuerza mayor debidamente justificado ante la Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería.
quote_translation: Art. 119. Every person holding temporary residence must remain in Salvadoran territory for a minimum of ninety calendar days within each year, whether consecutive or accumulated, save where there is fortuitous event or force majeure duly justified before the Directorate General of Migration and Foreign Nationals.
data_change_needed: The 90-day figure is confirmed but has nowhere to land: the atlas holds no El Salvador residence rows at all. Authoring at least one El Salvador temporary residence row is the prerequisite, carrying physical_presence_days_per_year: 90. Note the rule is general to ALL temporary residents rather than attached to a single programme, so it applies to every El Salvador temporary residence row authored in future. Two further recordable facts from the same decree: new art. 164 makes children under eighteen born abroad BEFORE their parents acquired Salvadoran nationality by naturalisation or nacionalización Salvadoran on the parents' application, with a duty to confirm on majority — this bears on el-salvador-citizenship-by-parent; and new art. 279 sets the causes of loss of naturalised Salvadoran nationality (residing more than two consecutive years in the country of origin, absence from El Salvador for more than five consecutive years without permission, or final conviction for serious intentional offences, the last being unrecoverable), which is A4 material for a future El Salvador dual_nationality block, currently null.
notes: Confirmed on the decree itself, fetched from the Legislative Assembly. The companion amendment verifies at the same URL: art. 1 substitutes numeral 5 of art. 49 so that failure to meet the ninety days becomes a ground of loss of temporary residence — '"5) Teniendo residencia temporal, no permanezcan en el territorio nacional por un período mínimo de noventa días calendario dentro de cada año, ya sean estos consecutivos o acumulados."' The consolidated law text confirms the reform landed: art. 119 in the Assembly's consolidated Ley Especial de Migración y de Extranjería now carries the reform marker (3), and the footnote table identifies (3) as D. L. N° 531, 17 DE MARZO DE 2026. NOT VERIFIED, and the lead should not be published with this figure: the 'from nine months' predecessor. Decreto 531 substitutes art. 119 outright without reciting the prior text, and the Assembly serves only the consolidated law, so the pre-2026 wording of art. 119 was not obtainable. The Diario Oficial download portal at diariooficial.gob.sv is a JS-driven DataTables application and the 2019 gazette issue was not reachable by direct URL. State the new rule, not the delta. Two dates in the lead are also off: the reform was approved 17 March 2026, not 11 March, and it took effect 31 March 2026. FETCH MECHANICS, and this row WILL show as 'HTTP 0' in research:verify:quotes — the failure is transport, not provenance. The quote WAS verified character-for-character against this exact URL using the gate's own extraction and normalisation (curl, then pdftotext -layout -enc UTF-8, then NFC plus whitespace collapse); the companion art. 49 quote verified the same way. The gate cannot reach the host itself: asamblea.gob.sv serves a leaf certificate with no intermediate, WebFetch rejects it with 'unable to verify the first certificate', and Bun's fetch does not error but HANGS, so fetchOnce returns status 0 on both the first attempt and the retry. The existing curl fallback in scripts/lib/quote-gate.ts only fires when the note matches INCOMPLETE_CHAIN, which a hang does not, so the fallback never runs. This is the same class of gap the gate's own comments record for almeezan.qa and adilet.zan.kz; widening the fallback to cover a transport hang would fix it, but that is a tooling change and is deliberately not made here. Alternative source investigated and REJECTED: the Diario Oficial's own issue PDF is directly addressable at https://www.diariooficial.gob.sv/seleccion/31728 (found via POST to https://www.diariooficial.gob.sv/api/v1/diarios-disponibles with year and month, whose response maps a date to an Id), and it is the right issue — Tomo N° 450, Numero 57, 23 de marzo de 2026, whose index lists 'Decreto No. 531.- Reformas a la Ley Especial de Migración y de Extranjería' at pages 3 to 6. But it is a 'NO VALE / SOLO PARA CONSULTA' consultation copy whose watermark is interleaved into the extracted text, and the decree body on pages 3 to 6 yields no extractable text at all, so no quote can be gated from it. Do not swap the source for it. Decree discovery is by POST to https://www.asamblea.gob.sv/leyes-y-decretos/resultado-busqueda/ with palabras_interes plus the four tiposdecreto GUIDs; results carry no hrefs, the detail page id is in a data-al-modal-url attribute. The PDF URL recorded above is a plain GET and stable. Discovery source was the Assembly's own press release at https://www.asamblea.gob.sv/node/13888, which is official but is a press release rather than the instrument; it confirms the 90 days and the amended article numbers.

claim_summary: Ethiopia established a 10-year golden visa programme requiring minimum direct investment of USD 10 million, or USD 5 million with substantial local job creation, alongside a USD 10,000 processing fee.
instrument: None found. No proclamation, Council of Ministers regulation, Federal Negarit Gazeta reference, directive or fee schedule was located.
quote_original: Investors can apply for various types of business visas that that vary from 30-days to 12-months.
notes: No Ethiopian primary source supports the claim, and two official surfaces contradict it by silence. Record nothing: under the no-negatives rule the absence belongs in this note, not in a row. The discovery source is unusable on its face — literally 'https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=' with no video id, and YouTube would not be authority even if complete. What was checked. The Immigration and Citizenship Service (ics.gov.et), the agency that would issue such a permit, publishes a service catalogue containing business visa, Ethiopian Origin ID with by-marriage and under-18 variants, NGO work permit, Permanent Residence ID, renewal of residence permit, student visa, temporary ID and temporary residence permit through marriage — no investor, golden or ten-year category, and that list matches the two Ethiopian rows the atlas already holds (ethiopia-origin-id-yellow-card, ethiopia-permanent-residence-id). Its Amharic news feed is current through August 2026 with items dated 6, 7, 13, 14, 16, 21, 25, 29 and 30 July 2026, straddling the claimed 8 July effective date, and not one concerns an investor or golden visa.
